newsitem.title: FRANCE: Send troops to protect aid workers - EU Parliament.
newsitem.headline: Send troops to protect aid workers - EU Parliament.

text.p: The European Parliament lashed out on Thursday at the international community's delay in sending troops to eastern Zaire to get aid to refugees.
It urged EU leaders meeting in Dublin on Friday and Saturday to discuss the issue "as a matter of priority".

The assembly said it deplored the way divisions within the European Union, U.S. reluctance to send soldiers and the unwillingness to cooperate of governments in the region were hindering the deployment of military protection for aid workers trying to reach hundreds of thousands of refugees.

"The stalemate in the situation in eastern Zaire is further proof of the lack of political will, both of members of the U.N. Security Council, which seems unable to take any operational steps, and of the EU, which lacks initiatives and a comprehensive approach," the parliament said in a resolution.
EU aid chief Emma Bonino accused the West of indifference towards the "missing" refugees, who are cut off from all aid and endagered by ongoing fighting in the Kivu region.

"We're being told 'there's only about 200,000 people involved, lost in Kivu'. So there's a new criterion in humanitarian conventions whereby a tolerance threshold is now 200,000. Or is it 300,000 or 400,000?"
"That's what worries me. And it worries me that nobody's talking about it any more," Bonino told the assembly.
"Nobody's authorised to go into Kivu, whether it be humanitarian organisations or in particular the media...If there are no headlines in newspapers indifference reigns," she said.
Bonino said the European Commission backed the Euro-deputies' call for the 14 countries who have promised troops to agree on action when they meet on Friday.

"We have actually won time to keep people alive so other people can find political solutions but nobody has shown the political will to do anything to find political solutions during that time," the Italian commissioner angrily told Euro-MPs.
Aid agencies and the U.S. military estimate that up to 600,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees have returned to Rwanda since November, but the whereabouts of some 700,000 others is a mystery.
Aid workers had to leave the area because of the fighting and Zairean rebels have not allowed them in since, although they agreed in late November to allow assessment work to begin.
